name: Online Safety and Responsible AI Use
objectives: For your main email account, create a strong passphrase, turn on two-step sign-in and check your phone and apps for updates, without help, with backup codes saved privately
Given a message or call, including AI voice or video, identify the warning signs of phishing and AI-powered scams, getting at least 4 of 5 right
When you meet a scam or your information is stolen, list where to report it and the first steps to protect yourself, naming all three U.S. reporting places

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Strong passwords and two-step sign-in
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a strong passphrase and turn on two-step sign-in for your email.
This lesson builds toward: For your main email account, you will create a strong passphrase, turn on two-step sign-in and check your phone and apps for updates, without help, with backup codes saved privately.
Your email is the key to everything: if someone gets into it, they can reset your other passwords. Protect it first.
A strong password is long and unique. An easy way is a passphrase: four or more random words, like "maple-river-tiger-lamp". Use a different password for every important account. A password manager, built into many phones and browsers, can remember them for you.
Turn on two-step sign-in, also called multifactor authentication or MFA. After your password, you also enter a code from your phone or approve a prompt. Even if someone steals your password, they still cannot get in. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) recommends strong passwords, MFA, a password manager and keeping software updated.
Step by step:
- Make a passphrase of four or more random words.
- Change your email password to it.
- Open your email account's security settings.
- Turn on two-step sign-in (MFA) and follow the steps.
- Save the backup codes somewhere safe and private.
Words to know:
- Passphrase: a password made of several random words.
- MFA / two-step sign-in: a second check, like a phone code, after your password.
- Password manager: a secure app that stores your passwords.
Official sources:
- CISA: Cybersecurity Awareness and Secure Our World
Try it now: Change your main email password to a strong passphrase and turn on two-step sign-in. If you cannot do it now, write down the steps and do it today.
You can now create a strong passphrase and protect your email with two-step sign-in.

check.q: Why protect your email account first?
options: It has the most photos
It is the hardest to use
Someone in your email can reset your other passwords
Email accounts cost money
check.why: Your email is the key to other accounts, because password resets go there.

check.q: Your job site password is the same as your email password. What do you do?
options: Make a different strong passphrase for each one
Keep it; one password is easier
Write it on your phone case
Share it with a friend to remember
check.why: Use a different password for every important account.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Spotting phishing and AI-powered scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Recognize phishing messages, fake calls and deepfakes before you click or pay.
This lesson builds toward: Given a message or call, including AI voice or video, you will identify the warning signs of phishing and AI-powered scams, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Phishing is a fake message, by email, text or social media, that tries to get you to click a link, share information or send money. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) lists common signs: a message you did not expect from a company you know, a claim of a problem with your account or payment, a request to confirm personal information, and a link to "update" your payment.
AI makes scams more convincing. Scammers can write perfect messages, make fake videos called deepfakes and copy a person's voice from a short clip. A call may sound exactly like your grandson, your boss or a parole officer.
Warning signs stay the same: they rush you, scare you, ask for gift cards, wire transfers or crypto, or ask for a code sent to your phone. Stop. Do not click. Contact the person or company using a number or website you already know is real.
Step by step:
- Pause: is this message unexpected or urgent?
- Do not click links or open attachments.
- Look for requests for money, gift cards, crypto or codes.
- Contact the person or company using a number you already know.
- Report it and delete it.
Words to know:
- Phishing: a fake message that tries to steal information or money.
- Deepfake: a fake video, image or voice made with AI to look or sound real.
- Voice cloning: using AI to copy someone's voice.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to recognize and avoid phishing scams
Try it now: Look through your email and text messages for one that could be phishing. List the warning signs it shows. With your family, agree on a safe word to check emergency calls.
You can now spot phishing, deepfake and voice-clone scams and respond safely.

options: A safe message from your bank
A way to back up your phone
A type of password
A fake message that tries to get you to click, share information or send money
check.why: Phishing is a fake message that tries to trick you.

check.q: A call sounds just like your parole officer and says to pay a fee today by wire transfer. What do you do?
options: Pay right away so you are not in trouble
Hang up and call the office on a number you already know
Give them the code sent to your phone
Call back the number that called you
check.why: Voices can be copied with AI; rushing and wire transfers are warning signs, so call a number you know.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reporting scams and recovering from identity theft
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List where to report scams and the first steps to take if your information is stolen.
This lesson builds toward: When you meet a scam or your information is stolen, you will list where to report it and the first steps to protect yourself, naming all three U.S. reporting places.
Reporting helps stop scammers and can help you recover. In the U.S., the FTC says to forward phishing emails to reportphishing@apwg.org, forward scam texts to 7726 (SPAM), and report fraud at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
If you gave away a Social Security, credit card or bank account number, the FTC says to go to IdentityTheft.gov for steps based on what was lost. Act fast: call your bank, change passwords, and consider a fraud alert or credit freeze.
If you clicked a bad link, update your security software, run a scan and remove anything it flags. Outside the U.S., report to your national police cybercrime unit or consumer protection agency.
Step by step:
- Phishing email: forward to reportphishing@apwg.org.
- Scam text: forward to 7726.
- Fraud: report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
- Information stolen: follow IdentityTheft.gov and call your bank.
- Clicked a link: update security software and scan.
Words to know:
- Identity theft: when someone uses your personal information to pretend to be you.
- Credit freeze: a lock that stops new credit being opened in your name.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to recognize and avoid phishing scams
- IdentityTheft.gov
- ReportFraud.ftc.gov
Try it now: Write the three U.S. places to report scams (or your country's equivalents) on a card or in your phone's notes.
You can now report scams and take the first steps after identity theft.

check.q: Where does the FTC say to go if your Social Security number was stolen?
options: IdentityTheft.gov
Any website with a phone number
The person who stole it
A social media group
check.why: The FTC points people to IdentityTheft.gov for steps based on what was lost.

check.q: You gave your bank card number to a fake website. What do you do first?
options: Wait to see if anything happens
Post about it online
Call your bank right away and change your passwords
Give the site your PIN too
check.why: Act fast: call your bank and change passwords.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Protecting privacy when you use AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Decide what is safe to type into an AI tool and what is not.
This lesson builds toward: Before you send a prompt to an AI tool, you will check the prompt and remove private information, sharing no passwords, ID, case, bank or card numbers.
What you type into an AI chat may be stored and, depending on the tool and settings, used to improve it. Treat it like talking in a public place.
Never type: passwords, Social Security or ID numbers, bank or card numbers, case or inmate numbers, medical details tied to your name, or other people's private information. Use placeholders like "[my number]" or general descriptions instead.
Look in the tool's settings for privacy and data controls, such as turning off chat history or training on your chats where offered. At school or work, use only the AI tools your school or employer allows, and follow their rules about what information can go in.
Step by step:
- Read your prompt before sending.
- Remove private numbers, names and medical details.
- Use placeholders like "[my number]".
- Check the tool's privacy settings.
- At school or work, use only approved tools.
Words to know:
- Privacy settings: options that control what an app saves and shares about you.
- Placeholder: a stand-in like "[my number]" instead of real private details.
Try it now: Open the settings of an AI assistant you use and find its privacy or data controls. Then rewrite this prompt safely: "My SSN is 123-45-6789, help me fill out this form."
You can now keep private information out of AI tools and use their privacy settings.

check.q: Typing into an AI chat is most like what?
options: Writing in a locked diary
Talking in a public place
Talking to your lawyer
Whispering to yourself
check.why: What you type may be stored, so treat it like talking in public.

check.q: You want AI help with a housing form that asks for your case number. What do you type?
options: Your real case number
Your case number and date of birth
Your friend's case number
A placeholder like "[my number]"
check.why: A placeholder gets you help without sharing private numbers.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checking AI for errors and bias
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check an AI answer for mistakes and unfair bias before you use it.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI answer, you will check it for wrong facts and unfair bias, before you use it.
AI can be confidently wrong. It can invent facts, quotes, laws or sources, which is called a hallucination. Always check facts that matter with an official or trusted source.
AI can also be biased: it learned from human writing, which includes unfair stereotypes. It might describe nurses as women and engineers as men, or treat people differently by name, age, race, disability or a criminal record. In hiring, lending, housing or schooling, that can cause real harm.
Test it: ask the same question with one detail changed, such as a different name, and compare the answers. If the AI treats people unfairly, do not use that answer, and report it using the tool's feedback button.
Step by step:
- Find the facts in the answer and check them with a trusted source.
- Look for stereotypes or unfair assumptions.
- Ask again with one detail changed and compare.
- Do not use unfair or wrong answers.
- Report problems with the tool's feedback button.
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when AI states something false as if it were true.
- Bias: unfair treatment or assumptions about a group of people.
- Stereotype: an oversimplified belief about a group.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to "describe a typical nurse and a typical engineer." Look for stereotypes. Then ask it to write a job reference for "Maria" and again for "James" with the same details, and compare.
You can now check AI answers for errors and test them for unfair bias.

options: When AI runs slowly
When AI uses big words
When AI treats groups of people unfairly or uses stereotypes
When AI answers in a list
check.why: AI learned from human writing, so it can repeat unfair stereotypes.

check.q: AI gives you a rule about voting after a conviction. What do you do before you rely on it?
options: Check it with an official or trusted source
Trust it because it sounds sure
Share it with friends first
Ask the AI if it is sure
check.why: AI can invent rules; check facts that matter with an official source.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Using AI honestly at school, work and online
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Follow the rules for AI use and be honest about when you used it.
This lesson builds toward: At school, at work or online, you will follow the rules for AI use, say how AI helped and choose when not to use AI, in a five-line personal AI rules card.
Rules about AI differ. Some teachers allow AI for brainstorming but not for writing; some jobs require it; some forbid it. Ask or read the rules first. Passing off AI work as your own where it is not allowed is cheating and can cost you a grade, a job or a certificate.
Be honest. If AI helped, say how when it matters: "I used an AI assistant to check grammar." Never use AI to make fake reviews, fake documents, or images or videos of real people without their consent. Making sexual or embarrassing fake images of real people is harmful and, in many places, illegal.
Know when not to use AI: emergencies (call 911), serious health, legal or money decisions (talk to a professional), and anything where you would not want your words stored. You are responsible for what you send or post, even if AI wrote it.
Step by step:
- Read or ask about the AI rules at your school or job.
- Use AI only in the ways allowed.
- Say how AI helped when it matters.
- Never make fakes of real people or documents.
- Skip AI for emergencies and big decisions.
Words to know:
- Academic honesty: doing your own work and giving credit for help you used.
- Consent: a person's permission.
Try it now: Final task: finish your safety checklist (passphrase, two-step sign-in, updates, report places) and write a five-line personal AI rules card covering privacy, checking answers, honesty, fairness and when not to use AI.
You can now protect your accounts, avoid and report scams, and use AI safely, honestly and fairly.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Email locked down The email password is short or reused, or two-step sign-in is off. The email password is a strong passphrase and two-step sign-in is on. Backup codes are saved privately and other important accounts have their own passwords. Updates checked The phone and apps were not checked for updates. The phone and apps were checked and updated. Automatic updates are turned on where offered. Reporting places Fewer than three reporting places written down. Wrote down 7726 for texts, reportphishing@apwg.org for emails and ReportFraud.ftc.gov for fraud. Also wrote IdentityTheft.gov and the first steps if information is stolen. Personal AI rules card Fewer than five lines, or a line is missing privacy or honesty. Five lines covering privacy, checking answers, honesty, fairness and when not to use AI. Each line gives a real example from the learner's own life. Privacy in prompts The rules card or practice prompts include private numbers. No private numbers anywhere, and placeholders are used. The learner checked their AI tool's privacy settings. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Who is responsible for a message you post that AI wrote?
options: The AI company
Nobody
The website
You
check.why: You are responsible for what you send or post, even if AI wrote it.

check.q: Your training program does not allow AI on the final test. What is the honest choice?
options: Use AI quietly
Follow the rule and do the test yourself
Ask a friend to use AI for you
Copy an AI answer and change a few words
check.why: Using AI where it is not allowed is cheating and can cost you the certificate.
